headline: Core inflation climbed to 3.3% in October and growth was revised up to a 4.3% pace, keeping a Fed hike on Dec. 9 firmly in view.
dateline: Thursday, November 26, 2026 · closes as of Wed Nov 25

rundown.h: Growth got revised up to a 4.3% pace.
rundown.p: The second estimate put third-quarter GDP growth at a 4.3% annualized rate, well above the 3.5% forecast and the 3.4% first print. Private investment jumped 22.4%, which Trading Economics ties to AI spending, and consumer spending grew 4.2%. Inventories added about 1.6 points, so final demand was a bit softer than the headline, but it is not the picture of an economy that needs relief.

rundown.h: Layoffs are still nowhere to be found.
rundown.p: Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 in the week ended Nov. 21, under the 200,000 forecast and down from 202,000. Continuing claims dropped to 1.697 million from 1.792 million, and the four-week average eased to 196,000. A labor market this tight keeps paychecks flowing, but it also gives the Fed cover to keep tightening.

rundown.h: The Beige Book says costs are outrunning prices.
rundown.p: Eight of the Fed's 12 districts reported slight to moderate growth, with consumer spending little changed and housing and construction weaker. Prices rose moderately, with firms citing energy, transport, healthcare, insurance and tariffs. Input costs are rising faster than selling prices, and contacts expect both to keep climbing: a recipe for thinner margins into 2027.

rundown.h: Dell doubled its revenue on AI servers.
rundown.p: Dell's fiscal third-quarter revenue hit a record $54.9 billion, up 103%, as AI-optimized server sales rose 291% to $22.0 billion. It booked $60.2 billion of AI orders, ended with a $132.3 billion AI backlog, raised its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion from $192 billion and added a $25 billion buyback. The AI build-out's hardware bill is still growing.

rundown.h: Factory orders cooled more than expected.
rundown.p: Durable goods orders rose 0.2% in October, short of the 0.6% forecast, after a 2.0% gain in September (revised from 1.9%). Excluding transportation, orders rose 0.5%. Business equipment demand is still growing, just more slowly than the AI headlines suggest.

rundown.h: Fewer shoppers are expected this holiday weekend.
rundown.p: The NRF expects 182.7 million people to shop from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, slightly below its 186.9 million forecast a year ago. Black Friday stays the big day, with 126 million planning to shop, and 59% of shoppers plan to use AI tools. Gift card spending is forecast at $26.8 billion, the lowest since 2015.

dive.title: Loan officers are tightening. Loan books aren't shrinking.
dive.dek: The Fed's latest loan officer survey shows banks pulling back on construction and nonbank lenders, even as balances keep growing.
body: Ask bank loan officers how they feel and the answer is: more careful. The Fed's October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, published Nov. 2 and covering the third quarter, found banks tightened standards on all three commercial real estate categories at once, something they last did in the third quarter of 2024. Construction and land development took the hardest hit, with a net 15.5% of banks tightening, per TheStreet's read of the survey. Large banks tightened on all three for the first time since late 2023, after six surveys of easing on construction and multifamily.

Demand is softening too. A net 25.9% of banks reported weaker demand for construction loans and 22.8% for multifamily, according to the National Association of Home Builders. On business loans, standards barely moved for big companies but tightened a bit for small firms, and about 12% of banks, net, saw weaker demand, the first weak readings since mid-2025. The Fed said banks pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain outlook. The sharpest pullback was toward nonbanks: a net 22% tightened on loans to private credit lenders, even as more of those lenders asked for money.

Yet the balance sheets tell a different story. The Fed's H.8 data, released Nov. 20, show total bank loans grew at an 8.9% annualized pace in October, with business loans up 11.7% and commercial real estate up 5.1%, the fastest of the past three periods. One explanation is that borrowers are drawing on lines and extending loans they already have, rather than banks writing fresh deals. The data don't settle that question.

For industrial owners, the split matters. Credit for stabilized buildings is tighter at the margin but available. Credit for new ground-up projects is getting scarcer, and the private lenders who often fill that gap are now facing tighter terms from banks themselves. That tends to slow new supply. What would change the picture: a Fed that stops hiking, or a January survey showing standards easing again.

rows: Net banks tightening: nonfarm nonresidential CRE
Net banks tightening: loans to private credit lenders

items.title: October core PCE rose to 3.3% a year, a tenth above forecasts, while real spending stalled

chart.t: Core PCE prices, % change from a year earlier
chart.src: Source: BEA via FRED (PCEPILFE), y/y calculated from the index

body: Core PCE prices, which strip out food and energy, rose 0.3% in October, matching September and the forecast, but the annual rate climbed to 3.3% from 3.1%, above the 3.2% consensus. Headline PCE rose 0.3% on the month, down from 0.5%, and 3.8% from a year earlier, in line with forecasts. Adjusted for inflation, consumer spending was flat after a 0.1% gain.

A year ago core PCE was running at 2.7%; it has climbed above 3% since March and is now at its highest of the past 14 months. On a quarterly basis, core prices rose at a 2.5% annualized pace in the third quarter, down from 3.3% in the second.

The report landed alongside an upward GDP revision. The AP said the inflation data added to Wall Street's worries, though Treasury yields fell on the day, and Trading Economics reports markets are pricing a December rate hike.

experts.view: In a Nov. 16 preview it expected a 25 bp hike in December and argued markets overprice a half-point move, seeing headline inflation peak this quarter as oil eases.
Before the release it estimated core at 3.3% a year, called that clearly hawkish and said it would meet Governor Waller's bar for 50 bp, though it still expected 25 bp.

items.lean: Pre-release previews from Oxford Economics and BofA both expected a quarter-point hike in December rather than a half point.
items.src: Sources: Trading Economics (core and headline PCE, Nov 25); FRED/BEA; AP via La Nacion; Oxford Economics; TheStreet Pro.

lead.title: The Houthis take aim at Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery
lead.body:
Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest, and caused fires. The Saudi-led coalition said air defenses intercepted four drones over Ras Tanura and did not say the refinery was hit, but NASA satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed thick smoke over roughly 600 square kilometers around the site.

The Houthis also claimed strikes on Riyadh's financial district; Saudi civil defense said 11 people were hurt Tuesday when the building housing the Public Investment Fund's headquarters was hit. A Houthi projectile also landed at Jazan port on the Red Sea, causing minor damage. There was no independent confirmation that refining or crude shipments were suspended.
lead.reach: Oil, again. Ras Tanura can refine 550,000 barrels a day; Brent rose above $95 on Nov. 26 for a third straight gain, yet is still down nearly 20% this month (Trading Economics).

views.view: They said rising risks to Saudi production are keeping prices afloat, but noted past attacks on Saudi facilities added premiums that faded once throughput recovered.
It projects a fourth-quarter supply surplus as Gulf shipments recover, which has capped the rally, as cited by Trading Economics.

reading.title: Own the best, short the worst, and know when to walk away
reading.dek: Tiger Management's founder built a hedge fund giant on a simple long-short idea, then closed it in March 2000 rather than chase a market he no longer understood.
body: Julian Robertson's core idea was almost disarmingly simple: find the best businesses you can and own them, find the worst and sell them short. If your winners can't beat your losers, he argued in various forms, you are in the wrong line of work. The long-short structure meant Tiger Management's results leaned on stock selection rather than on which way the overall market happened to move. Shorts were a hedge, but also a second source of returns.

The record made the case. The North Carolina native, a former Kidder Peabody stockbroker, launched Tiger in 1980 with roughly $8 million from family, friends and his own pocket. From inception to its 1998 peak, the fund compounded at about 31.7% a year after fees, against roughly 12.7% for the S&P 500, and posted losses in only four of its 21 years. Assets swelled to about $22 billion by mid-1998, making it one of the largest hedge fund groups in the world.

Then the framework collided with a market that stopped rewarding it. A wrong-way bet on the Japanese yen in 1998 and a large, struggling stake in US Airways hurt returns, and redemptions followed. Meanwhile Robertson deliberately stayed light on technology as dot-com shares soared. Over about 18 months, losses and withdrawals shrank assets to around $6 billion. In March 2000, close to the very top of the bubble, he shut his six funds and handed outside capital back to investors. His letter conceded that he no longer understood the market, insisted such manic stretches had come and gone before, and maintained that value investing remained the right course.

The timing looks prescient in hindsight, yet the lesson is subtler than calling the top. Robertson did not abandon his discipline; he declined to keep risking clients' money in a regime where fundamentals seemed disconnected from prices. Knowing when your edge has temporarily stopped working, and stepping aside rather than drifting from your process, is its own form of risk management. So is admitting it publicly, instead of quietly loosening your standards to chase whatever is working.

His other legacy is human. Robertson trained and later seeded a generation of managers known as the Tiger Cubs, including Lee Ainslie, Stephen Mandel, Andreas Halvorsen, John Griffin and Chase Coleman, often taking a stake in their firms in return. Not every cub thrived; Bill Hwang's Archegos imploded in 2021. Robertson died in August 2022 at 90, having given away more than $2 billion.

quote.text: …risk in a market which I frankly do not understand.
quote.src: Julian Robertson, March 2000 letter to Tiger investors (via Fortune, 2022)

takeaways: In a choppy AI tape, stock picking on both sides matters more than the index.
With a 10-year near 4.9%, cash pays you while you wait.
If prices stop making sense, cut risk rather than loosen your standards.
